decision.case_name: Capital Standard, LLC v. U.S. Bank National Association
decision.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Second District
decision.retrieved_from: Florida Courts published PDF (flcourts-media.flcourts.gov); found via CourtListener cluster 10954406
decision.ai_tool_found: generative AI tool, unidentified; the court found counsel used one "from the beginning of this appeal without any apparent guardrails"
decision.scale_note: The court's show-cause order documented forty-six hallucinations in total (thirty-one in the amended initial brief, fifteen in the reply). The opinion itemises only the samples reproduced below.

url_check.mirror_url: 202, zero-byte Cloudflare bot challenge (courtlistener.com blocks automated fetchers)

offending.quoted_text: [u]nder Florida law, a party's actions that affirm the validity of a transaction preclude subsequent challenges to that transaction
offending.court_quote: Repeatedly citing Maciejewski v. Holland, 441 So. 2d 703 (Fla. 2d DCA 1983), a two-page opinion explaining why the complaint there stated a cause of action for declaratory relief, for unrelated propositions such as that “[u]nder Florida law, a party's actions that affirm the validity of a transaction preclude subsequent challenges to that transaction” …
offending.what_actually_exists: Maciejewski v. Holland, 441 So. 2d 703 (Fla. 2d DCA 1983) is a real two-page opinion explaining why the complaint there stated a cause of action for declaratory relief. U.S. Bank pointed out that it “does not even mention the word ‘ratification’ (let alone the concept).”

offending.quoted_text: [r]atification occurs when a party, through its actions or inactions, affirms a transaction or fails to repudiate it within a reasonable time.
offending.court_quote: … for unrelated propositions such as … that “[r]atification occurs when a party, through its actions or inactions, affirms a transaction or fails to repudiate it within a reasonable time.” … In its answer brief, U.S. Bank pointed out that Gonzalez says nothing whatsoever about a noteholder's rights and that Maciejewski does not even mention the word “ratification” (let alone the concept).
offending.what_actually_exists: Maciejewski is real but does not mention ratification at all.

offending.as_cited: Hart Properties, Inc. v. Slack, 159 So. 2d 236, 239 (Fla. 1963)
offending.quoted_text: [fundamental error] goes to the foundation of the case or the merits of the cause of action and is equivalent to a denial of due process
offending.court_quote: Serving up nonexistent quotes—complete with purported pincites—such as, “[fundamental error] goes to the foundation of the case or the merits of the cause of action and is equivalent to a denial of due process,” citing Hart Properties, Inc. v. Slack, 159 So. 2d 236, 239 (Fla. 1963).
offending.what_actually_exists: Hart Properties, Inc. v. Slack, 159 So. 2d 236 (Fla. 1963) is a real Florida Supreme Court decision; the quotation with its pincite is nonexistent.

offending.as_cited: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst, 641 So. 2d 467 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994)
offending.cited_case_name: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst
offending.quoted_text: Florida law provides strong protections to individuals who acquire property in good faith, for valuable consideration, and without notice of competing claims
offending.court_quote: Passing off Miami Country Day School v. Bakst, 641 So. 2d 467 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994), a case discussing the statutory mechanics of whether a houseboat qualified for a homestead exemption, as authority for a panoply of propositions, including that “Florida law provides strong protections to individuals who acquire property in good faith, for valuable consideration, and without notice of competing claims” …
offending.what_actually_exists: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst, 641 So. 2d 467 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994) is real and discusses the statutory mechanics of whether a houseboat qualified for a homestead exemption.

offending.as_cited: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst, 641 So. 2d 467 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994)
offending.cited_case_name: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst
offending.quoted_text: a party's delay or misleading conduct bars recovery where another party suffers detriment as a result
offending.court_quote: … as authority for a panoply of propositions, including … that “a party's delay or misleading conduct bars recovery where another party suffers detriment as a result.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Miami Country Day School v. Bakst is a homestead-exemption case about a houseboat.

offending.as_cited: Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., 95 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012)
offending.cited_case_name: Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co.
offending.quoted_text: substantive evidence, not speculation, is needed to rebut possession-based presumptions
offending.court_quote: Relying on Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., 95 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012), a case pertaining to the adequacy of an undated assignment to confer standing, as an all-purpose authority on a multitude of other subjects, including that “substantive evidence, not speculation, is needed to rebut possession-based presumptions” …
offending.what_actually_exists: Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., 95 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012) is real and concerns the adequacy of an undated assignment to confer standing; U.S. Bank pointed out it “says nothing whatsoever about a noteholder's rights.”

offending.as_cited: Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., 95 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012)
offending.cited_case_name: Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co.
offending.quoted_text: good faith reliance on recorded documents is sufficient to establish bona fide purchaser status
offending.court_quote: … as an all-purpose authority on a multitude of other subjects, including … that “good faith reliance on recorded documents is sufficient to establish bona fide purchaser status.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Gonzalez concerns the adequacy of an undated assignment to confer standing.

offending.as_cited: Board of Regents v. Wilson, 365 So. 2d 213 (Fla. 1st DCA 1979)
offending.court_quote: Capital Standard's reply brief added another fifteen AI hallucinations, including the fake case Board of Regents v. Wilson, 365 So. 2d 213 (Fla. 1st DCA 1979); citations to several of the offending cases from the amended initial brief for additional propositions that are nowhere to be found in them; and, for good measure, citations to several new cases with that same problem.

controls.as_cited: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
controls.cited_for: that a federal district court sanctioned attorneys and a law firm under Rule 11 for citing fake cases created by generative AI
controls.court_quote: It's been three years since the release of the widely publicized decision in Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), in which a federal district court sanctioned several attorneys and a law firm under rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure for, among other things, citing fake cases created by generative artificial intelligence.

controls.as_cited: Fletcher v. Experian Info. Sols., Inc., 168 F.4th 231, 235 (5th Cir. 2026)
controls.cited_case_name: Fletcher v. Experian Info. Sols., Inc.
controls.cited_for: that it is no longer an excuse to plead ignorance of the risks of using generative AI to draft a brief without verifying its output
controls.court_quote: See Fletcher v. Experian Info. Sols., Inc., 168 F.4th 231, 235 (5th Cir. 2026) (“If it were ever an excuse to plead ignorance of the risks of using generative AI to draft a brief without verifying its output, it is certainly no longer so.”).

controls.as_cited: United States v. McGee, 806 F. Supp. 3d 1264, 1275 (S.D. Ala. 2025)
controls.cited_for: that no attorney can claim ignorance of the problem with AI-generated cases and authorities
controls.court_quote: see also United States v. McGee, 806 F. Supp. 3d 1264, 1275 (S.D. Ala. 2025) (“Given the broad attention . . . to the problem with AI generated cases and authorities, no attorney can claim ignorance or simply bury their head in the sand when it comes to their own use of AI (regardless of what program they use).”).

controls.cited_for: that Rule 11 requires attorneys to read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the authorities on which they rely
controls.court_quote: cf., e.g., Park v. Kim, 91 F.4th 610, 615 (2d Cir. 2024) (“At the very least, the duties imposed by [Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11] require that attorneys read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the legal authorities on which they rely.”).

controls.as_cited: Boca Burger, Inc. v. Forum, 912 So. 2d 561, 571 (Fla. 2005)
controls.cited_for: that appellate courts depend on counsel to accurately state both the facts and the applicable law
controls.court_quote: Boca Burger, Inc. v. Forum, 912 So. 2d 561, 571 (Fla. 2005) (“[Appellate courts] depend on counsel to accurately state both the facts and the applicable law.”).

controls.as_cited: Whiting v. City of Athens, 170 F.4th 455, 461 (6th Cir. 2026)
controls.cited_for: that it does not matter that some of the cases cited exist or that some propositions were legitimate
controls.court_quote: Moreover, it does not matter that “some of the cases” that Attorney Keefe cited exist or that “some of the propositions of law were legitimate.” See Whiting v. City of Athens, 170 F.4th 455, 461 (6th Cir. 2026).
